To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
exposure to airborne particulate fractions of PM, CP, FP and UFP, induces time- and size-specific OxS and inflammation in lung and aortic tissue in a rat model.
exposure to airborne particulates induces oxidative stress (OXS) and inflammation in lung and aortic tissue in a particle size- and time dependent manner.
exposure to particulate matter induces lung injury, oxidative stress and inflammatory response.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying the adverse health effects associated with exposure to PM.
the biological mechanisms underlying the adverse effects of PM exposure.
the biological effects of airborne particulate matter and their possible implications in the etiology of cardiovascular diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the biological mechanisms of the transient oxidant toxic effects are particle size and exposure time dependent.
the biological mechanisms underlying OxS and inflammation associated with acute lung injury and cardiovascular alterations are particle size and dose-dependent exposure.
the biological effects of PM are dependent on particle size and exposure time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
exposure to PM is associated with oxidative stress in both the lungs and the cardiovascular system.
OxS is a common pathway for PM to induce lung injury and vascular dysfunction.
the oxidative stress and the inflammation are the main mechanisms of lung damage induced by the exposure to particulate matter, which later reaches cardiovascular system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the size of airborne particulates is an important determinant of OxS in the lung and aorta, and the effects are time-dependent.
the size of the particulates is the main determinant of their biological effects, and this is the reason why the UFP are considered the most toxic.
OxS is a common pathway in the lung and aorta and that FP and UFF are the major contributors in the induction of OxSp and inflammation.
